intro: This branch covers statistics (collecting, summarizing, and picturing data) and probability (how likely something is to happen). These skills help people read surveys, charts, and news claims with a sensible, questioning eye.

III.9.01.what: A statistical question is one whose answer varies, so you need to collect data to answer it.

levels.a: Tells a statistical question apart from one with a single answer.
levels.b: Expects many different answers to a statistical question.
levels.c: Picks the best-worded statistical question on a topic.
levels.d: Decides what data to collect to answer a question.

III.9.02.what: The mean (average) is what each value would be if everything were shared out equally.

levels.a: Evens out stacks of cubes to see the mean as a fair share.
levels.b: Finds the mean by adding the values and dividing by how many there are.
levels.c: Works out the score needed next to reach a target average.
levels.d: Sees how one unusual value, an outlier, pulls the mean up or down.
levels.e: Works backwards: knows the mean and all but one value, finds the missing value.
levels.f: Works out which number was removed, from the mean before and after.

III.9.03.what: The median is the middle value when data are in order; the mode is the most common value.

levels.a: Orders a list and finds the middle value.
levels.b: Finds the median of an even-sized list by averaging the two middle values.
levels.c: Finds the mode, and knows a list may have none.
levels.d: Decides whether the mean or the median better describes a typical value.
levels.e: Finds the missing value that makes the mean and the median of a list equal.
levels.f: Finds the largest number a list could contain, given its mean, median and mode.

III.9.04.what: The range is the gap between the largest and smallest values, a simple measure of spread.

levels.a: Finds the range, including data with negative numbers.
levels.b: Finds the range from a dot plot.
levels.c: Sees how one extreme value can stretch the range.
levels.d: Compares the ranges of two sets of data.

III.9.05.what: Quartiles split ordered data into four equal parts; the interquartile range (IQR) is the spread of the middle half.

levels.a: Splits ordered data into a lower half and an upper half.
levels.b: Finds the lower and upper quartiles, the middles of each half.
levels.c: Finds the interquartile range by subtracting the lower quartile from the upper.
levels.d: Uses a standard rule based on the IQR to decide which values are outliers.

III.9.06.what: A box plot is a chart that shows the spread of data using five key numbers.

levels.a: Finds the five key numbers: smallest, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, largest.
levels.b: Picks the box plot that matches five given numbers.
levels.c: Reads values like the median from a box plot.
levels.d: Compares two box plots to decide which statements are true.

III.9.07.what: A dot plot shows each data value as a dot above a number line.

levels.a: Picks the dot plot that matches a list of data.
levels.b: Reads the median and range from a dot plot.
levels.c: Describes the shape: where the peak is and which value stands apart.
levels.d: Answers questions from a dot plot, like how many had 4 or more.

III.9.08.what: A histogram is a bar chart of data grouped into ranges, like ages 10 to 19, 20 to 29.

levels.a: Chooses sensible equal-width groups that cover all the data.
levels.b: Counts how many values fall in each group to set each bar's height.
levels.c: Reads how many values are in a group from the chart.
levels.d: Describes the shape as balanced or lopsided to one side.

III.9.09.what: Mean absolute deviation measures how spread out data are: the average distance of the values from the mean.

levels.a: Finds how far each value is from the mean.
levels.b: Averages those distances to find the mean absolute deviation.
levels.c: Explains what a larger or smaller mean absolute deviation says about consistency.
levels.d: Compares the spread of two sets of data.

III.9.10.what: Sampling means surveying a smaller group to learn about a whole population.

levels.a: Tells the sample (who is surveyed) from the population (everyone of interest).
levels.b: Picks a method that gives a fair, random sample.
levels.c: Spots a biased sample, one that leans toward certain answers.
levels.d: Knows larger random samples give more trustworthy estimates.

III.9.11.what: Using results from a sample to make estimates about the whole population.

levels.a: Finds the fraction of a sample with some feature.
levels.b: Scales a sample result up to estimate a whole population.
levels.c: Combines several samples for a better estimate.
levels.d: Recognizes that samples vary, and draws a conclusion that allows for this.

III.9.12.what: Comparing two groups using their typical values and how spread out they are.

levels.a: Compares the medians of two groups.
levels.b: Compares the spread of two groups using box plots.
levels.c: Measures the gap between two means in units of their typical spread.
levels.d: Writes a fair conclusion about which group scored higher.

III.9.13.what: Probability measures how likely something is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

levels.a: Knows a probability must lie between 0 and 1.
levels.b: Describes an event as impossible, unlikely, likely, or certain.
levels.c: Finds a probability as the number of ways it can happen over the total number of outcomes.
levels.d: Finds the chance something does not happen by subtracting from 1.
levels.e: Works backwards from a probability to find how many marbles of the other color are in a bag.
levels.f: Works out how many marbles to add to a bag to change the chance of red to a target.

III.9.14.what: Experimental probability is estimated from what actually happens when you repeat something many times.

levels.a: Records the results of repeated trials in a tally.
levels.b: Finds the fraction of trials with a given result.
levels.c: Compares actual results with what theory predicts.
levels.d: Knows that more trials usually give results closer to the true chance.

III.9.15.what: A sample space is the full list of possible outcomes, such as every result of tossing two coins.

levels.a: Picks the complete list of outcomes.
levels.b: Uses a table to list all outcomes of two events together.
levels.c: Uses a tree diagram, a branching picture, to count outcomes.
levels.d: Multiplies the number of choices at each stage to count all possibilities.
levels.e: Counts codes where no digit can be used twice, multiplying one fewer choice each time.
levels.f: Counts every three-digit number whose digits add up to a set total.

III.9.16.what: Finding the probability of two things happening, such as rolling a 6 and drawing a vowel card.

levels.a: Multiplies probabilities for two events that don't affect each other.
levels.b: Finds a probability by counting in a table of all outcomes.
levels.c: Tells apart the chance of "this and that" from "this or that."
levels.d: Solves word problems, like picking two marbles with replacement.
levels.e: Finds the chance of picking two marbles in a row without putting the first one back.
levels.f: Finds a chance with two dice, like getting a total that is a multiple of 4, by careful counting.

III.9.17.what: A simulation uses coins, dice, or random numbers to act out a situation and estimate a probability.

levels.a: Picks a random device that matches a given chance.
levels.b: Plans how random digits will stand for outcomes in each trial.
levels.c: Runs a simulation from a list of random digits and counts results.
levels.d: Estimates a probability from the simulation results.

III.9.18.what: A scatter plot shows pairs of data as dots, to see whether two things are related.

levels.a: Finds the dot that shows a given pair of values.
levels.b: Describes whether the two go up together, go opposite ways, or show no link.
levels.c: Spots clusters and dots that stand apart from the rest.
levels.d: Decides whether the pattern follows a straight line or a curve.

III.9.19.what: A trend line is a straight line drawn through a scatter plot to show the overall pattern and make predictions.

levels.a: Picks the line that best fits the dots, by eye.
levels.b: Writes the equation of a trend line.
levels.c: Uses a trend line's equation to make a prediction.
levels.d: Explains what the slope and starting value of a trend line mean.

III.9.20.what: A two-way table counts people or things sorted two ways at once, such as grade and whether they play an instrument.

levels.a: Reads counts and totals from a two-way table.
levels.b: Fills in missing counts so rows and columns add up.
levels.c: Turns counts into percents within one row or column.
levels.d: Decides whether the two ways of sorting are linked.
